overview: This Ava record spans 1650 to 1783: the later restored Toungoo or Nyaungyan kingdom, its fall in 1752, and early Konbaung rule. It does not represent medieval Ava. The imported outline stays identical through three map snapshots, including the southern coast, despite major political changes. Read it as broad geographic context, not a reliable border throughout these years.

periods.title: Later restored Toungoo kingdom
periods.summary: Ava was an inland royal and commercial center connected with lower-river ports. Dutch records illuminate seventeenth-century trade.

periods.title: Collapse and Konbaung reconstruction
periods.summary: Pegu’s conquest ended the Nyaungyan dynasty. Alaungpaya’s resistance established a different royal house.

sections.title: A capital connected by water and trade

items.text: Ava stood where the Myitnge meets the Irrawaddy, near the irrigated rice lands of Kyaukse. A canal linked the rivers around the city. Water helped connect royal government, farming and transport: feeding a capital depended on much more than what grew inside its walls.

In 1752 forces from Pegu captured Ava and ended the Nyaungyan dynasty. Their victory did not secure lasting obedience from Upper Burma’s local leaders. Aung Zeya, later called Alaungpaya, organized resistance from Moksobo and founded the Konbaung dynasty. The city’s familiar name outlasted the defeated royal house.

Dutch East India Company records open an unusually detailed window onto seventeenth-century commerce. Its main Burma office was at Syriam, with a subsidiary at Ava. Surviving inventories and accounts record fabrics, prices and wages. These business papers preserve traces of customers and workers who rarely appear in royal monuments.

Many buyers wanted affordable Indian cloth of medium or coarse quality, rather than only royal luxuries. Imported red cotton yarn was valued for its lasting color and could be mixed with local yarn in weaving. A thread in a household’s clothing could therefore connect local work with distant Indian producers.

Large glazed Martaban jars carried water, rice and even gunpowder aboard ships. A pot could be part of the shipping equipment, not merely something sold at the destination. Before standardized metal containers, a very big jar could do a surprisingly important transport job.

An order dated 16 March 1680 demanded rice or paddy from more than 200 villages in an irrigated district. Religious and service lands had exemptions. Such documents show government tracking fields and households while claiming a share of the harvest.

A 1691 order addressed which hereditary service groups children of marriages between different groups should enter. Family relationships could shape compulsory duties to rulers and institutions. These classifications remind us that royal society included severe restrictions on personal freedom.

In 1715 Hla Myat San, formerly of the palace entertainment group, received a title after marrying a royal uncle. She was permitted gold containers for betel and pickled tea. Even the snack dishes could announce someone’s newly elevated rank.

The seventeenth-century Leidatgyi temple borrowed from Bagan’s Ananda temple. Its builders used radial vaulting, tiers of windows and elaborate stucco; seated lions guarded a doorway. Looking backward could be a creative choice: earlier religious architecture remained a model for later craftspeople.

Across the river, the Kaunghmudaw pagoda was already standing when this map interval begins: it was founded in 1636. Its great rounded dome is surrounded by 812 stone pillars with niches for oil lamps. Imagine preparing that many little places for light.

Religious murals can contain a bustling world of ordinary work. The Ava-period survey identifies people fishing, plowing and making pots, as well as contemporary clothing and houses. Painters placed sacred stories in recognizable surroundings, leaving clues about the material world around their viewers.

Dating a painted building takes detective work. Tilokaguru’s murals were long discussed using a 1672 date. Later research challenged that chronology and connected the paintings with early seventeenth-century evidence, before this record begins. A building’s foundation story and the date of its paintings must be checked separately.

sections.title: Learning, health and a royal message

items.text: Late eighteenth-century Upper Burmese monasteries taught boys, novices and junior monks through Pali and bilingual texts. Regular study included grammar, monastic discipline and Buddhist philosophy. Learning involved mastering languages and categories, not simply hearing stories; the evidence describes particular institutions rather than schooling available equally to every child.

In 1783 a minister asked the scholar Ñāṇābhivaṃsa which works of worldly knowledge could no longer be found in Burma. He identified 48 previously available titles. This was a serious missing-books list: rulers and scholars were trying to recover texts through wider Indian Ocean connections.

A history published by Myanmar’s traditional-medicine department identifies U Myat Tun of Khwe Saung village, south of Ava, as the author of a prose medical manual dated 1133 Myanmar Era, in the early 1770s. Its subjects included childbirth, infant illnesses, fever and diarrhea. The list records the family health problems its author sought to address.

Alaungpaya’s Golden Letter of 7 May 1756 names Ava as “Ratanā-pūra-Aṅwa-prañ-krī,” translated as “royal city of Ratanapura-Ava.” This is the scholarly Roman transliteration of Burmese written on the surviving gold letter, not a modern phrase invented for this page. Its royal voice belongs to the new Konbaung dynasty.

ending.text: The Nyaungyan dynasty ended in 1752, but Konbaung rule continued beyond this map record. In 1783 Bodawpaya moved the royal residence from Ava to Amarapura. A change of dynasty and capital did not erase the region’s communities.
